1. Introduction and summary

1.1 About this document

This good practice guidance has been produced by the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government (MHCLG) Homelessness and Rough Sleeping Youth Adviser Team and the Department for Education (DfE) Care Leaver Policy Team to support local authorities to develop and strengthen joint housing protocols, enabling care-experienced young people to access and maintain suitable accommodation through coordinated, high-quality practice.

A joint housing protocol should help children’s services and housing authorities deliver their local accommodation offer to care-experienced young people and prevent homelessness. It sets out commitments that local authorities, as corporate parents, should adopt and how these will be delivered in practice.

This guidance is not issued with the status of statutory guidance. It provides information and advice drawn from good practice and offers a framework which local authorities and partners can use when developing their joint housing protocols.

In the statutory Homelessness Code of Guidance, the Secretary of State for Housing, Communities and Local Government and the Secretary of State for Education, expect that all housing authorities, children’s services authorities and other relevant departments within local authorities, develop joint housing protocols and procedures to ensure that each department plays a full role in providing united corporate parenting support to young people leaving care.

For the purposes of this guidance, the term ‘care-experienced’ is used to describe young people who may, in legal terms, be classified as Former Relevant Children or persons qualifying for advice and assistance. The term care leaver is only used when directly referring to legislative phrasing.

What this guidance does

This guidance supports local authorities and partners to:

understand the purpose of a joint housing protocol for care-experienced young people

strengthen joint working between children’s services, housing authorities and relevant partners

plan accommodation early so homelessness does not become the default route into housing

align joint housing protocols with corporate parenting responsibilities, local offers, homelessness support and relevant statutory guidance

set out clear local arrangements for accommodation pathways, contingency planning, escalation and dispute resolution

use data, young people’s feedback and regular review to improve practice and outcomes

1.2 Relevant legislation and statutory guidance

This document refers to the following legislation:

Housing Act 1996 - Part 6 (Allocations) and Part 7 (Homelessness), as amended by the Homelessness Reduction Act 2017

Homelessness (Priority Need for Accommodation) (England) Order 2002

Children Act 1989

Children (Leaving Care) Act 2000

Children and Social Work Act 2017 - sections 1, 2 and 3

The following is a list of statutory guidance that this document refers to:

Homelessness code of guidance

Applying corporate parenting principles to looked after children and care leavers

Children Act 1989: care planning, placement and case review

Children Act 1989: transition to adulthood for care leavers

Extending Personal Adviser support for all care leavers to age 25

Local offer guidance

The legislation and statutory guidance above should be read together. For ease of use, the key duties and expectations most relevant to joint housing protocols are summarised thematically below.

Corporate parenting duties

Corporate parenting duties provide the overarching framework for joint housing protocols. The Children and Social Work Act 2017 sets out the corporate parenting principles that local authorities must have regard to when supporting looked after children and care leavers. These include promoting wellbeing and stability, taking account of young people’s views, helping them access services, promoting high aspirations, and preparing them for adulthood and independent living.

The Homelessness Code of Guidance also emphasises the importance of housing authorities, children’s services authorities and other relevant departments working together to provide united corporate parenting support to young people leaving care. The Children’s Wellbeing and Schools Act 2026 further strengthens this approach by extending corporate parenting responsibilities to a wider range of public bodies and all government departments. From Autumn 2027, public bodies in scope will become corporate parents, with new duties requiring them to play an active role in supporting children in care and care leavers. For joint housing protocols, this means local authorities should consider how wider partners are engaged where their services, decisions or statutory functions affect accommodation planning, homelessness prevention, transition to adulthood, tenancy sustainment or support for care-experienced young people leaving custody.

Staying Close

Priority need

Under homelessness legislation, certain care leavers have a priority need for accommodation. This includes young people aged 18, 19 or 20 who were looked after between the ages of 16 and 18. The Homelessness Code of Guidance is clear that this applies whether or not the young person qualifies for leaving care services from children’s services.

For care leavers aged 21 or over, priority need is not automatic. Housing authorities must assess whether the person is vulnerable as a result of having been looked after, accommodated or fostered. In carrying out this assessment, housing authorities should take account of the guidance in Chapter 8 and Chapter 22 of the Homelessness Code of Guidance, including the length of time the person was looked after, the reasons they were looked after, the time since they left care, whether they have been able to obtain and maintain accommodation, and the support networks available to them.

Housing authorities should take particular care when assessing whether a care leaver aged 21 or over is vulnerable. This should include consideration of whether, if homeless, they would be at particular risk of exploitation, abuse or involvement in offending behaviour as a result of their care experience.

The joint housing protocol should set out how housing and children’s services will work together to support priority need assessments for care leavers aged 21 or over. This should include arrangements for sharing relevant information, with consent, about the young person’s care history, support needs, vulnerabilities, accommodation history and existing support networks. Personal Advisers, advocates and other trusted professionals should be involved where appropriate, so that assessments are informed by a full understanding of the young person’s circumstances.

Where there is a potential that a care leaver does not have a priority need, the protocol should set out how services will jointly plan next steps. This should include clear arrangements for ongoing accommodation and support, escalation where needed, and contingency planning to reduce the risk of repeat homelessness, deterioration in the young person’s circumstances or rough sleeping.

Intentional homelessness

The joint housing protocol should reflect that from 30 September 2026, an intentional homelessness decision cannot be made where the applicant is a care leaver in scope of the corporate parenting duty. The exemption does not apply retrospectively. The housing authority must consider if the cause of their current homelessness took place from 30th September 2026, and if at that point they were an exempt care leaver. An exempt care leaver will not benefit from the exemption if the cause of their current homelessness occurred before 30th September 2026; whereas a person who was an exempt care leaver on becoming homeless after the effective date will not be intentionally homeless.

The protocol should instead set out how housing and children’s services will work together to support care leavers where there is a risk of accommodation loss or where homelessness occurs. This should include:

how services will take all reasonable steps to prevent the loss of accommodation where a care leaver is at risk, including early identification of issues and coordinated support

arrangements for escalating concerns to senior leaders in housing and children’s services where a care leaver’s accommodation is at risk due to their actions or wider circumstances

how housing and children’s services will work together to agree crisis and contingency accommodation arrangements where the loss of accommodation cannot be prevented.

how services will work together to identify and plan for care leavers approaching age 25, to avoid a cliff edge in support. This should include early review of accommodation, support needs and tenancy sustainment arrangements before statutory leaving care support comes to an end, recognising that the risk of repeat homelessness or rough sleeping may increase if support reduces or ends without a clear transition plan

how senior leaders from housing and children’s services will jointly review and agree future accommodation and support plans, ensuring:

a clear understanding of the reasons for the loss of previous accommodation

that appropriate support is in place to meet the care leaver’s needs

that accommodation is suitable and sustainable

that there are planned review points to support the success of the placement

2.11 Dispute resolution

The protocol should set out clear routes for escalation and resolving disputes between services where there is disagreement about the support and accommodation provided to a care-experienced young person, including where they may be homeless or threatened with homelessness.

This should include:

clear stages of escalation between housing and children’s services, including when and how issues should be raised and reviewed

identification of named roles or senior leads responsible for resolving disputes at each stage

clear criteria for when disputes should be escalated, including where there is a risk of homelessness, delay in decision-making, or disagreement about duties owed

expected timescales for resolving disputes, particularly where there is a risk to the young person’s accommodation or wellbeing

a requirement that disputes are resolved in line with corporate parenting responsibilities, ensuring that the needs and best interests of the young person remain central to decision-making

a complaint process for young people, with access to advocacy

Training/taster flats: Short term training flats can help care-experienced young people test and gain a sense of the responsibilities that come with independent living, and experience the reality of living alone, which may identify other challenges such as loneliness, isolation and accessing support.

Living with family: Some care-experienced young people choose to live with immediate or extended family. The protocol should set out how suitability, safety and sustainability are assessed, what support is available to the young person and family, and how contingency planning will reduce the risk of homelessness if arrangements break down.

Support for young parents: Protocols should also include the specialist accommodation available to care-experienced young people with children or who are pregnant, how they are supported to access this accommodation and longer term move-on options.

Suitability of accommodation

Local authorities must ensure that accommodation provided for care leavers is suitable for their needs. The protocol should explain who assesses suitability, how decisions are made and reviewed, and how young people can raise concerns or challenge decisions with advocacy support where appropriate. Relevant suitability guidance is set out in Children Act 1989 care planning guidance and the Homelessness Code of Guidance. Key considerations include:

Accommodation should be matched to need, including risk, support requirements, location, affordability and the young person’s ability to sustain the placement or tenancy.

Bed and breakfast accommodation is not suitable for care leavers and should only be used in exceptional circumstances as a last resort, with senior oversight, active monitoring and a clear plan to move the young person to suitable accommodation as quickly as possible.

Protocols should set out how suitability concerns are escalated and how young people can access advocacy, complaints or review routes.

Protocols should also reflect relevant quality standards for supported accommodation used for 16- and 17-year-old looked after children and care leavers.

Referral routes

The protocol should explain how access to supported accommodation is managed, including referral routes, prioritisation, matching to vacancies, and the role of any single point of contact or gateway. Local authorities, providers and partners should seek to avoid duplicated assessments and make the process as seamless as possible for young people.

2.5 Joint contingency planning

Effective contingency planning helps care-experienced young people avoid homelessness, rough sleeping and avoidable accommodation breakdown. The joint housing protocol should set out how Children’s Services, Housing Services, commissioned providers and relevant partners will identify risk early, act quickly, and work together to sustain accommodation wherever possible.

Contingency planning should focus on situations where a care-experienced young person’s accommodation may be at risk, including where there are concerns about rent arrears, anti-social behaviour, relationship breakdown, provider withdrawal, eviction, safeguarding risk, or a planned placement ending without a suitable move-on option. Arrangements should be particularly clear for care-experienced young people who may have complex needs, limited informal support, previous placement instability, or experience of the criminal justice system.

The protocol should set out local arrangements for:

early warning signs or trigger points that require joint review

how concerns are shared between housing, children’s services, providers and the Personal Adviser, with the young person’s consent where required

how the Pathway Plan and any accommodation or support plan will be reviewed where accommodation is at risk

the role of multi-agency panels, placement panels or other local forums in reviewing higher-risk cases

the support that can be put in place to sustain accommodation, including mediation, restorative work, budgeting or tenancy support, increased floating support, practical help, or adjusted support arrangements

how decisions to evict, withdraw accommodation or end a placement will be reviewed and escalated before final action is taken

when senior oversight is required from both housing and children’s services

how a managed move or alternative suitable accommodation will be planned if the current arrangement cannot be sustained

Where eviction, withdrawal of accommodation or placement breakdown is being considered, the protocol should encourage joint senior review before a final decision is taken. This should test whether all reasonable steps have been taken to sustain the accommodation, whether additional or adjusted support could make the arrangement suitable, and what the impact of accommodation loss would be on the young person’s welfare, stability and future housing outcomes.

Where the loss of accommodation cannot be avoided, housing and children’s services should agree a joint plan to secure alternative suitable accommodation without delay. This should include support before, during and after the move, named lead officers, review points, and contingency arrangements to reduce the risk of repeat breakdown. Local areas may wish to use the senior oversight template at Annex B to support this process.

Example from practice: tenancy sustainment and early escalation

Haringey’s protocol provides a useful example of how contingency planning can involve the wider range of partners needed to support tenancy sustainment, including those responsible for tenancy management, housing support and escalation where risks emerge.
